prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The depth map supports a layered ground-plane layout: nearby hands, containers, and the pale board or pole are brightest at roughly 0.3–1 m, while the standing people and bowls are generally about 1–2 m away and the upper background is farther, roughly 2–4+ m. It clarifies that several bowls and containers lie below and in front of the people, with nearby objects often separated from one another by about 0.3–1 m; the diagonal pole extends from the camera wearer’s near foreground toward the middle distance. Across the five frames, lateral shifts mostly reflect the camera turning across the same workspace, while the people remain at broadly similar depth rather than clearly approaching or retreating. The map also exposes foreground occlusions and objects cut by the lower and side borders, but its absolute metre estimates are uncertain, bright regions are sometimes saturated, and boundaries around people, vessels, and thin poles are smeared or merged.
descriptions.segmentation: The segmentation map isolates several partly visible people and a few objects—three person instances, two bowls, and one cell phone—making their identities and left/right placement clearer than in the cluttered RGB scene. The people occupy the left side in the first frames and the far right in the last frame, mostly about 1–2 m from the camera wearer by comparison with the depth map; the detected bowls sit lower or near the top-middle of their frames, roughly 0.5–1.5 m away and within about an arm’s length of nearby people. Large portions of every person extend outside the upper or side image boundaries, and the masks show where bodies overlap or are occluded by the frame edge, although they do not reliably indicate facing direction or eye contact. The detections change abruptly across frames because many visible bowls, containers, poles, and body regions are missed, the cell-phone label appears spatially questionable, and the coloured instances are not tracked consistently through time.
descriptions.pose: The pose map is entirely black in all five frames, so it supplies no body or hand keypoints and supports no reliable estimates of limb position, facing direction, gaze, reach, or person-to-person spacing. In the RGB strip, people are partly cropped at the top and sides and some hands are small or occluded by objects, conditions that plausibly leave the pose representation without usable detections. Consequently, it cannot reveal any approach, retreat, turning, reaching, or changing occlusion that is difficult to see in RGB alone. Its main spatial indication is therefore negative and unreliable: no skeleton was recovered even though people and hands are visibly present.
